subject: Polynomial curve-fitting with two dependent variables

messages.author: 8b78a79c64716511
messages.subject: Polynomial curve-fitting with two dependent variables
parts:
Hello, ggplot2 gurus,

I have a dataset consisting of two dependent variables and one independent variable, like so:

measures<-data.frame(A=c(28.
27, 65.32, 139.00, 179.28, 176.56, 93.25), B=c(141.38, 130.63, 139.00, 89.64, 35.31, 151.41), p=c(7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 16))

abplot<-ggplot(measures, aes(A, B))+geom_point()

In this case, the error variances are approximately equal for both A and B, and both are measured in the same unit.  When I've added together A and B and regressed them against the third (independent) variable, p, a second-order polynomial fit has higher explanatory power than a linear fit.

My question is this: the default method for geom_smooth() uses ordinary least squares regression to minimize variance on y (right?).  Is it somehow possible to add the appropriate polynomial curve to this graph - one that minimizes variance on both x and y?

Thank you in advance for any insights,

Rebecca Clark

-
Postdoctoral Researcher
Entomology Department
Texas A&M University
College Station, TX 77843

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Polynomial curve-fitting with two dependent variables
parts: Hi:

On Tue, Apr 24, 2012 at 3:38 PM, Rebecca Clark <rebecc...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello, ggplot2 gurus,
>
> I have a dataset consisting of two dependent variables and one independent
> variable, like so:
>

B=c(141.38, 130.63, 139.00,
> 89.64, 35.31, 151.41), p=c(7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 16))
>
> abplot<-ggplot(measures, aes(A, B))+geom_point()
>
> In this case, the error variances are approximately equal for both A and B,
> and both are measured in the same unit.  When I've added together A and B
> and regressed them against the third (independent) variable, p, a
> second-order polynomial fit has higher explanatory power than a linear fit.

I had to read this a couple of times before I think I got it: is this
what you're looking for?

ggplot(measures, aes(x = p, y = A + B)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() +
geom_smooth(method = 'lm', colour = 'red', fill = 'red', alpha = 0.1) +
geom_smooth(method = 'lm', colour = 'blue', formula = y ~ poly(x, 2),
fill = 'blue', alpha = 0.1)

The advantage of adding the confidence bands to the plot is to show
that the quadratic model in p has tighter confidence bands than the
corresponding linear model. Observe that in the second call to
geom_smooth, the formula uses y as the response and x as the single
covariate rather than the actual names of the covariate and response.
poly(x, 2) fits a quadratic polynomial model in x.

>
> My question is this: the default method for geom_smooth() uses ordinary
> least squares regression to minimize variance on y (right?).  Is it somehow
> possible to add the appropriate polynomial curve to this graph - one that
> minimizes variance on both x and y?

Actually, the default method for geom_smooth() is loess, a popular
nonparametric smoother; try

ggplot(measures, aes(x = p, y = A + B)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() +
geom_smooth()

The resulting warnings indicate that loess seriously overfits these
data, which is evident from the plot generated by the above code.
(This is a consequence of the small sample size - it really makes no
sense to fit a loess model when n is this small.) The first and
second-order linear models in p both use OLS.

I don't know what your last parenthetical comment means - OLS
minimizes the residual sum of squares, but does not minimize variance
in either x or y (except perhaps by coincidence).

HTH,
Dennis

parts:
Hi Dennis,

Thank you so much for taking a crack at this, and apologies for being overly cryptic.  That's what I get for trying to be concise, I suppose. :-)

I'd managed the same set of linear fits on the plot of p vs. A+B, so that wasn't quite what I was looking for - what I was hoping to do was to translate that fit onto the scatterplot of A vs. B alone.  I realize it's a little bit silly, but people in my field are most accustomed to looking at A and B plotted against each other. 

As you note, OLS minimizes the residual sum of squares, which is essentially an effort to minimize variation in y for a given x.  What I meant to say I was looking for is to minimize the *total* least squares (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_least_squares) because there is variation in both x and y.  I suspect I might have to dig into the syntax for stat_smooth() to accomplish that goal, but was hoping that maybe someone else had run into the same problem and had come up with a solution.

Thanks again,
Rebecca Clark

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Polynomial curve-fitting with two dependent variables
parts:
I can't answer your question about using TLS, but once you have the TLS model object, it's possible to plot the line without using stat_smooth() -- in fact, it's probably a better idea to not use stat_smooth() in a case like this because it's hard to make sure that it's using the same model that you generate yourself.

Generally speaking, model objects have an associated predict() method. For example, lm objects have predict.lm(); glm objects have predict.glm(), and so on. The specific methods are called automatically when you pass the model object to the non-specific predict() method. Assuming that there's a predict method for tls, you could do something like this, replacing the model with whatever you come up with:


measures <- data.frame(

A=c(28.27, 65.32, 139.00, 179.28, 176.56, 93.25),
  B=c(141.38, 130.63, 139.00, 89.64, 35.31, 151.41),
  p=c(7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 16))

# Make the model - quadratic lm in this case
model <- lm(B ~ A + I(A^2), data=measures)

# Need to create a new data frame with predictor (A) values spanning the range
# of A from the original data in measures
minA <- min(measures$A)
maxA <- max(measures$A)
newdata <- data.frame(A = seq(minA, maxA, length.out=100))

# Predict values across the range
newdata$B <- predict(model, newdata)

# Plot the original points with a line of predicted values
ggplot(measures, aes(x=A, y=B)) + geom_point() + geom_line(data=newdata)


-Winston

Winston,

Aha, that's a good portion of the battle, thank you very much.  And I'm in complete agreement with you about plotting the line directly in lieu of stat_smooth, especially for a complex/potentially confusing case such as this one. 

I know that this is possible for a model II linear regression (with package lmodel2 - see http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6103288/reduced-major-axis-line-and-ci-for-ggplot-in-r).  So then all that's left is my statistical question about computing a model II polynomial regression, which isn't really a ggplot2 question any longer.

Thank you again to everyone who has chimed in - I've been listening in on the list for a while and have appreciated how helpful everyone is, and all of the assorted tips and tricks that have been shared.

-Rebecca Clark
